history.heading: Carantania and the Habsburgs
paragraphs: Slovenia lies where the Alps meet the Mediterranean and the Pannonian Plain. Slavic ancestors of the Slovenes settled there in the 6th century and formed the principality of Carantania. From the late Middle Ages most Slovene lands came under the Habsburgs, where they remained until 1918.
Primož Trubar printed the first Slovene books during the Protestant Reformation in the 16th century, and the poet France Prešeren helped shape national identity in the 19th century.

history.heading: Yugoslavia and independence
paragraphs: After the First World War, Slovenia joined the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes. During the Second World War it was divided among Germany, Italy and Hungary, and partisans resisted. After the war it became the most prosperous republic of socialist Yugoslavia.

Slovenia declared independence on 25 June 1991 and won a Ten-Day War against the Yugoslav army. It joined NATO and the EU in 2004, was the first former communist country to adopt the euro in 2007, and joined Schengen.

culture.heading: Language and nature
paragraphs: Slovene is a South Slavic language with an unusual "dual" grammatical form. Most Slovenes are Catholic. Over half the country is covered by forest, and landmarks include Lake Bled, the Postojna and Škocjan caves and the Julian Alps with Mount Triglav, a national symbol.

Beekeeping is a national tradition, and the Carniolan honey bee is native. Potica (nut roll) and kranjska klobasa (sausage) are traditional foods. Slovenia produces outstanding athletes, including basketball star Luka Dončić and Tour de France winners Tadej Pogačar and Primož Roglič.

politics.heading: Parliamentary republic
paragraphs: Slovenia is a parliamentary republic with a directly elected president and a prime minister responsible to the National Assembly. Governments are coalitions. Nataša Pirc Musar became the first female president in 2022.

economy.heading: High-income economy
paragraphs: Slovenia has one of the highest incomes among post-communist countries. Key sectors include pharmaceuticals, car parts, electrical appliances, logistics through the Port of Koper and tourism. It has relatively low inequality. The currency is the euro.
